sentences.text: Machaeroprosopus is an extinct pseudopalatine phytosaur from the Late Triassic, belonging to the family Parasuchidae and the subfamily Mystriosuchini.
The genus includes multiple species such as M. andersoni, M. buceros, M. jablonskiae, M. lottorum, M. mccauleyi, M. pristinus, and M. validus.

Most species formerly assigned to Machaeroprosopus have been reassigned to the genera Smilosuchus, Rutiodon, or Phytosaurus, while the genus Pseudopalatus is now considered a junior synonym of Machaeroprosopus.
M. jablonskiae is notable for having a well-preserved braincase, a feature rarely found in detail in phytosaur fossils.
The original skulls of M. validus were lost in the 1950s, leaving only a line drawing from the 1916 description as a visual record.
The specific name of M. jablonskiae honors Pat Jablonsky, who discovered the only known specimen.

The species M. validus was named in 1916 based on three complete skulls found in the Chinle Formation of Arizona, though the description originally cited a complete skull and two partial skulls from Coconino County.
M. andersoni was described by Maurice G. Mehl in 1922 based on a partial skull holotype.

M. buceros was originally named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1881 as Belodon buceros based on a partial skull, but recent research determined that the holotype of the genus Machaeroprosopus is actually M. buceros, not M. validus.
M. jablonskiae was described by Parker and Irmis in 2006 based on a posterior skull roof and braincase collected in September 2002 near Mountain Lion Mesa in Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona.
M. lottorum was named in 2013 by Axel Hungerbühler, Bill Mueller, Sankar Chatterjee, and Douglas P. Cunningham and is known from two complete skulls housed at Texas Tech University.

Machaeroprosopus mccauleyi was described in 1989 based on an incomplete skull missing the front part of the snout, and the species name honors the McCauley couple who owned the land where the holotype was discovered.
Machaeroprosopus pristinus was originally named in 1928 based on a nearly complete skull collected near Adamana, Arizona, from the Norian-aged Upper Petrified Forest Member.

Phylogenetic analysis suggests M. jablonskiae is the most basal species within the group formerly known as Pseudopalatus, while analysis indicates M. lottorum is a derived species closely related to Redondasaurus gregorii.
Recent research determined that the holotype of the genus Machaeroprosopus is actually M. buceros, not M. validus, confirming that the holotype is the species formerly known as Pseudopalatus buceros.
Machaeroprosopus lived during the Norian to Rhaetian stages of the Late Triassic, between 227.3 and 201.4 million years ago.
Specimens of M. andersoni were likely collected from the Bull Canyon Formation in Guadalupe County, New Mexico.
The holotype of M. buceros was collected from the Norian-aged Chinle Formation in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico.
Specimens of M. lottorum were collected 13 km south of Post in Garza County, Texas, from the Norian Cooper Canyon Formation.
The holotype of M. pristinus was collected near Adamana, Arizona, from the Norian-aged Upper Petrified Forest Member.
Machaeroprosopus was historically considered a doubtful name due to a lack of diagnostic specimens distinguishing it from other phytosaurs.
